messages.author: c044830b46c5e07f
messages.subject: Hierarchical Exponential Mixture Model
parts:
Good day, all,

I'm working on a project where times between events are theorized to be drawn from a mixture of of several exponential distributions with widely varying rate parameters, leading to a heavy-tailed distribution. We have data from several experiments of this sort ranging from ~14,000 to ~190,000 observations in each experiment and would like to sample the posteriors of the overall rate parameters for each of the component exponentials. Using Stan to fit an exponential mixture model was straightforward enough, though slow, to estimate the component rate parameters and their mixing proportions for individual experiments. Now where I'm stuck is extending this to a hierarchical form and sampling efficiently. I haven't found any examples of mixture models that don't involve looping through the entire data set (which in this case would be just over 700,000 observations), which I think is the cause of the slowness in sampling (I tried the model below with a subset of the data of 800 observations and took 2000 posterior samples and it took 4 hours to run). Is there some trick of vectorization I should try instead of this approach for fitting the mixture model?

Additionally, I'm not sure if I'm wildly off base with my approach to setting up the hierarchical priors. I figured a gamma prior on each exponential rate parameter would be ideal, and put flat positive priors on the shape and scale parameters of those gammas. I would then calculate mu[k] = shape[k] / scale[k] to estimate the posterior of the mean overall rate parameters. Does this seem reasonable or completely ridiculous?

Many thanks for any assistance you can provide,
Steven Kern


data {

    int<lower=1> N; // number of observations

    int<lower=1> G; // number of experiments

    int<lower=1> K; // number of mixture components

    int<lower=1,upper=G> group[N]; // index of experiments

    real y[N]; // outcome observations

}

parameters {

    simplex[K] pi;  // mixing proportions (shared across experiments)

    real<lower=0> shape_overall[K]; // overall gamma shape parameter

    real<lower=0> scale_overall[K]; // overall gamma scale parameter

    real<lower=0> lambda_ind[G,K]; // individual experiment level exponential rate parameters (K rates per experiment)

}

transformed parameters {

    real<lower=0> mu_overall[K]; // overall mean rate parameters

    for (k in 1:K) {

        mu_overall[k] <- shape_overall[k] / scale_overall[k];

    }

}

model {

    real ps[K];

    for (g in 1:G) {

        for (k in 1:K) {

            lambda_ind[g,k] ~ gamma(shape_overall[k], scale_overall[k]);

        }

    }

    for (n in 1:N) {

        for (k in 1:K) {

            ps[k] <- log(pi[k]) + exponential_log(y[n], lambda_ind[group[n],k]);

        }

        increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(ps));

    }

}

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Hierarchical Exponential Mixture Model
parts:
I’ll defer to Bob because he’s king of the mixture models.  Regarding your priors, sure, I guess gamma is fine. I often use lognormal just cos I understand it better.  Also, I strongly recommend you use informative priors; this could help a lot.
A

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Hierarchical Exponential Mixture Model
parts:
There are a couple of things you can do to speed this up.
See below.

> On May 29, 2015, at 10:31 AM, Steven Kern <kern.s...@gmail.com> wrote:
>

> I'm working on a project where times between events are theorized to be drawn from a mixture of of several exponential distributions with widely varying rate parameters, leading to a heavy-tailed distribution. We have data from several experiments of this sort ranging from ~14,000 to ~190,000 observations in each experiment and would like to sample the posteriors of the overall rate parameters for each of the component exponentials. Using Stan to fit an exponential mixture model was straightforward enough, though slow, to estimate the component rate parameters and their mixing proportions for individual experiments. Now where I'm stuck is extending this to a hierarchical form and sampling efficiently. I haven't found any examples of mixture models that don't involve looping through the entire data set (which in this case would be just over 700,000 observations), which I think is the cause of the slowness in sampling (I tried the model below with a subset of the data of 800 observations and took 2000 posterior samples and it took 4 hours to run). Is there some trick of vectorization I should try instead of this approach for fitting the mixture model?
>
> Additionally, I'm not sure if I'm wildly off base with my approach to setting up the hierarchical priors. I figured a gamma prior on each exponential rate parameter would be ideal, and put flat positive priors on the shape and scale parameters of those gammas. I would then calculate mu[k] = shape[k] / scale[k] to estimate the posterior of the mean overall rate parameters. Does this seem reasonable or completely ridiculous?
>
>

> data {
>
> int<lower=1> N; // number of observations
>
> int<lower=1> G; // number of experiments
>
> int<lower=1> K; // number of mixture components
>
> int<lower=1,upper=G> group[N]; // index of experiments
>
> real y[N]; // outcome observations
>
> }
>
> parameters {
>
> simplex[K] pi; // mixing proportions (shared across experiments)
>
> real<lower=0> shape_overall[K]; // overall gamma shape parameter
>
> real<lower=0> scale_overall[K]; // overall gamma scale parameter
>
> real<lower=0> lambda_ind[G,K]; // individual experiment level exponential rate parameters (K rates per experiment)
>
> }
Declare these as vector[K] and matrix[G,K].

> transformed parameters {
>
> real<lower=0> mu_overall[K]; // overall mean rate parameters
>
ditto.

> for (k in 1:K) {
>
> mu_overall[k] <- shape_overall[k] / scale_overall[k];
>
> }
>

Then you can use elementwise division:

mu_overall <- shape_overall ./ scale_overall;

Not much faster, if any, but less work.

> }
>
> model {
>
> real ps[K];
>
> for (g in 1:G) {
>
> for (k in 1:K) {
>
> lambda_ind[g,k] ~ gamma(shape_overall[k], scale_overall[k]);
>
> }

It'd be much better to go the other way around and declare

vector[G] lambda_ind[k];

and use a vectorized form like this:
for (k in 1:K)

lambda_ind[k] ~ gamma(shape_overall[k], scale_overall[k]);

because that way, you do all the computations on the parameters to
gamma only once for each k.

>
> }
>
> for (n in 1:N) {
>
> for (k in 1:K) {
>

> ps[k] <- log(pi[k]) + exponential_log(ADT[n], lambda_ind[group[n],k]);
>
> }
>
> increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(ps));
>
> }
>

Because you have this:

exponential_log(y, lambda) = log(lambda) - lambda * y;

you can precompute log_lambda_ind = log(lambda_ind) and log_pi = log(pi) and write
this all as:
for (n in 1:N)
ps <- log_pi;
for (k in 1:K)

ps[k] <- ps[k] + log_lambda_ind[group[n], k] - lambda_ind[group[n], k] * ADT[n, k];

I didn't see ADT defined anywhere in your program, though.

As Andrew said, you'll probably need some informative priors
at the hierarchical level to keep the lower-level estimates under
control.

- Bob
